notes: Partial-settlement credit insurance trial; single construction issue on Maximum Advance is clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Credit default insurance: meaning of Maximum Advance

statutes_considered.title: Consumer Credit (Rebate on Early Settlement) Regulations 1983

key_facts: College Credit Ltd (CCL) provided sub-prime motor finance insured by NIG under a credit default policy renewed until December 2002.
After partial settlement, the sole remaining issue was whether ADB and GAP customer insurance premiums counted towards the Underwriting Criteria Maximum Advance.
If those premiums were included, many agreements exceeded the cap and fell outside cover; Net Outstanding Balance expressly excluded such premiums from claims.
Hannington Bailey Associates acted as intermediary; HBA faced potential follow-on claims depending on the construction outcome.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial on a single coverage construction issue after partial settlement between CCL and NIG.
enrichment.outcome: Construction issue decided in favour of CCL; Advance for Maximum Advance purposes excludes ADB and GAP premiums.
enrichment.ratio: In this credit default policy, Maximum Advance means the payment made by CCL to the dealer to complete the purchase, excluding optional customer insurance premiums, because compliance with underwriting criteria should link insured credit risk to vehicle security rather than uninsured add-ons that could arbitrarily void cover.
legal_issues: Whether ADB and GAP premiums form part of Advance for Maximum Advance underwriting criteria
Whether textual or commercial purpose analysis governs where policy language is undefined
Practical effect of contingent maximum finance calculations on forecourt transactions
linked_authorities: Biggin v Permanite [1951] 2 KB 314

confidence.notes: Single construction point and outcome are explicit. HBA costs and follow-on claims were not finally determined.

notes: Appeal from summary judgment on share-sale indemnity; Holme v Brunskill and surrender defences rejected on clear facts.

enrichment.short_title: Share sale indemnity appeal over lease guarantee
key_facts: Eurodis guaranteed CEM's Belfast lease and later sold CEM shares to Unicomp Holdings under a share sale agreement with indemnity and guarantee clauses.
CEM went into liquidation; Unibol occupied the premises without formal assignment consent; Eurodis paid £290,000 to settle Fortwilliam's Northern Ireland claim.
Eurodis sued Unicomp Inc for indemnity under clauses 4.11 and 7.1 of the share sale agreement.
Unicomp argued surety defences including Holme v Brunskill discharge, surrender by operation of law, and failure of best endeavours to obtain release.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from summary judgment for £365,303.84 plus interest and costs.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; defences have no reasonable prospect of success.
enrichment.ratio: Fortwilliam's forbearance in enforcing lease covenants fell within the guarantee proviso and did not discharge Eurodis under Holme v Brunskill; continued rent payment by Unibol was not inconsistent with lease continuation; Holdings' indemnity obligation persisted pending release regardless of best endeavours performance.
legal_issues: Whether Unicomp was surety or indemnifier under the share sale agreement
Application of Holme v Brunskill to landlord forbearance on assignment covenant breaches
Whether acceptance of rent from Unibol operated as surrender releasing the guarantee
Whether Holdings failed to use best endeavours to procure Eurodis's release

Howard de Walden Estates Ltd v Pasta Place Ltd [1995] 1 EGLR 79

notes: Long procedural judgment on s23 CJA 1988; four granted grounds and additional summing-up defect all clearly analysed.

enrichment.short_title: Unsafe conviction: fearful witness statement under s23
key_facts: Lobban was convicted on retrial of possessing cocaine with intent to supply after drugs were found in Heather Moore's Fiesta and his fingerprints were on the ashtray.
At the first trial Judge Reynolds read Moore's statement under section 23 after excluding the defendant and denying defence cross-examination on voir dire.
The judge applied section 25 rather than section 26 and misunderstood the extent to which Lobban disputed Moore's account of car use.
At retrial the jury received inadequate directions on untested statement evidence and the judge failed to summarise Lobban's interview defence blaming Carl Dwyer.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction with leave on four grounds; court also treated failure to summarise defence as rendering conviction unsafe.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction quashed; retrial not ordered given time served.
enrichment.ratio: Where a witness's fear is in issue under section 23, fair procedure requires proper voir dire questioning including defence cross-examination unless exceptional protective measures are justified; statements prepared for criminal proceedings require section 26 leave criteria; juries must be warned about limited weight of unread and uncross-examined statement evidence.
legal_issues: Propriety of judge's room hearings and defendant exclusion during fear inquiry
Whether section 25 or section 26 governs admissibility of witness statements
Right to cross-examine witness on voir dire as to fear
Adequacy of jury directions on hearsay statement evidence
Duty to summarise defence case from interview

notes: Test-case appeal on MoD non-delegable duty; lengthy authority review but outcome and ratio are clear.

enrichment.short_title: MoD non-delegable duty for German hospital birth injury
key_facts: A child born in Germany to a British army family suffered cerebral palsy from negligent vacuum delivery at Gilead Krankenhaus.
After 1996 the MoD arranged secondary care through GST and designated German provider hospitals rather than British Military Hospitals.
German experts and Gutachter Kommission found negligence; Gilead insurers admitted liability and equivalent English damages were available in Germany.
The appeal tested whether the MoD owed a non-delegable duty to ensure careful obstetric treatment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from Bell J's Part 8 determination that no non-delegable duty was owed.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; MoD owed only a duty to provide access to an appropriate secondary healthcare regime by reasonable selection of providers.
enrichment.ratio: English law does not impose on the MoD a non-delegable duty to ensure due skill and care in German DGP treatment where it no longer operates hospitals itself; the duty is organisational—to exercise reasonable care in procuring access—and was discharged by contracting with GST; prior military hospital duty did not survive outsourcing.

Application of Australian hospital non-delegable duty jurisprudence
Effect of B's reasonable perception of Army-provided care
Whether pre-1996 duty persisted after closure of military hospitals

notes: Homelessness review procedural fairness appeal; statutory framework and Hobbs applied straightforwardly.

statutes_considered.title: Allocation of Housing and Homelessness (Review Procedure) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Ms Lomotey jointly owned a Valley House flat with her brother but surrendered her interest and accepted a notice to quit to seek council rehousing.
Enfield decided she was intentionally homeless under section 191; the review panel confirmed after refusing an oral hearing.
She had not included her partner David Whyte on her application though later submissions raised family life under Article 8.
The county court judge held the review procedurally unfair for failing to explore Whyte's position and collusion findings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Local authority appeal against county court decision quashing intentional homelessness finding for procedural unfairness.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; review procedure fair; intentional homelessness decision restored.
enrichment.ratio: Natural justice requires the substance of adverse points to be put to the applicant, not repetition in identical form; here collusion and Whyte's exclusion were fully explored in interviews and the application form itself showed she did not seek accommodation with him, so regulation 8(2) did not apply and no further oral hearing was required.
legal_issues: Whether review panel had to explore whether Lomotey wished to live with Whyte
Application of regulation 8(2) where reviewer saw no deficiency in original decision
Procedural fairness when credibility and collusion are in issue
Whether accommodation at Valley House was reasonable to continue to occupy

notes: Gwilliam/Bottomley analysis on contractor insurance duty; appeal allowed on orthodox competence standard.

enrichment.short_title: Nightclub owner not liable for uninsured doorman
key_facts: Payling suffered severe head injuries when ejected by a doorman at Naylor's Main Street nightclub in Rotherham.
Naylor engaged Whitehead's licensed security staff under a local Pub and Club Watch scheme for about eighteen months without incident.
Whitehead had no public liability insurance; the judge held Naylor breached duty by failing to check insurance cover.
The door attendant's negligence was admitted; the dispute was whether Naylor owed a free-standing duty to ensure insurance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from liability-only trial before HHJ Murphy.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; no free-standing duty to ensure contractor insurance; accredited long-used contractor satisfied competence duty.
enrichment.ratio: An occupier delegating security to an independent contractor is not generally under a free-standing duty to ensure public liability insurance; the duty is to take reasonable care in selecting a competent contractor, which may in some fact-specific cases include insurance checks, but here licensed accredited contractors with a satisfactory track record required no further inquiry.
legal_issues: Whether employer owed free-standing duty to ensure independent contractor had insurance
Distinction between competence and suitability of independent contractors
Application of Gwilliam v West Hertfordshire Hospitals NHS Trust
Effect of statutory licensing scheme on standard of care in contractor selection

enrichment.short_title: Walkinshaw personal indemnity for Arrows overdraft
key_facts: Tom Walkinshaw gave a personal indemnity capped at half of advances under a £13m Morgan Grenfell overdraft to Arrows Autosports Ltd.
The indemnity broadly defined Indemnified Persons including affiliates, associates, shareholders and partners of the Overdraft Provider MGDCS.
MGDCS was reimbursed by Morgan Grenfell equity funds partnerships which acquired the overdraft benefit in summer 2000.
Arrows collapsed owing the full overdraft; Walkinshaw resisted liability to the funds as indemnified persons.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial on remaining indemnity construction and quantum issues after Pumfrey J had rejected other Walkinshaw defences.
enrichment.outcome: Walkinshaw liable under indemnity to MGDCS claiming for Funds I–IV (and Fund V on commercial matrix analysis); liable for principal and contractual interest subject to cap.
enrichment.ratio: On proper construction of the widely drafted indemnity, the Morgan Grenfell equity funds partnerships were affiliates or associates of MGDCS within the financing matrix for Arrows; their loss from non-repayment of the overdraft related to MGDCS's advances and MGDCS may sue on their behalf; res inter alios acta does not let MGDCS ignore reimbursement when no own loss remained.

Whether Funds I–V are affiliates or associates of MGDCS

notes: Conflicting ownership judgments on Rallye aircraft; privity and Hodson v Walker principles applied with full reasoning.

enrichment.short_title: Aircraft title: prior purchaser not bound by earlier judgment
key_facts: Wiltshire as Spilsby Soaring Trust trustee claimed a Rallye aircraft sold without authority by Ebbs to Etherington, Heapy and Storey, then to Powell.
HHJ O'Rorke declared Wiltshire owner in proceedings against Ebbs alone after Ebbs's bankruptcy.
Powell bought in good faith before that judgment; Recorder Maw later declared Powell owner in separate proceedings.
Wiltshire detained the aircraft from Powell relying on the earlier declaration.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against declaration that Powell held good title despite prior judgment against Ebbs.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Powell not estopped by earlier judgment because he acquired title before judgment and was not a privy.
enrichment.ratio: Estoppel per rem judicatam binds privies in estate only if they derive title from the judgment debtor after the judgment; a purchaser of goods before judgment is not bound even where title passes through the unsuccessful litigant, because the vendor no longer represented that interest during the first action.
legal_issues: Whether subsequent purchasers of goods are privies estopped by judgment against their vendor
Whether privity requires acquisition of interest after judgment or after commencement of proceedings
Application of Hodson v Walker to chattels
Appropriate form of declaratory relief as to ownership

enrichment.short_title: Commercial Court retains insurance-heavy construction dispute
key_facts: Lumbermens Mutual Casualty sought a declaration on liability insurance coverage arising from Braehead shopping centre construction claims against Bovis.
The action combined important insurance law issues with substantial TCC-type building contract liability between Bovis and Braehead.
Bovis applied to transfer the case to the Technology and Construction Court citing trial length and TCC expertise.
Ascertainment and breach of warranty insurance points might dispose of the case without trying construction liability.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to transfer proceedings out of the Commercial Court to the TCC.
enrichment.outcome: Transfer refused; case to remain in Commercial Court with insurance issues tried first in 2004.
enrichment.ratio: Where core Commercial Court insurance construction issues—including ascertainment of liability under a liability policy—may determine the action without trying building contract liability, the case is not inappropriate for the Commercial Court despite substantial TCC factual issues; staged trial management under CPR overriding objective is preferable to transfer.

notes: Marine cargo inherent vice claim; Gaunt and Noten principles applied with detailed weather and engineering evidence.

enrichment.short_title: Transformer damage held inherent vice not all-risks loss
key_facts: A large Alstom transformer shipped from Ellesmere Port to Malaysia under a project all-risks marine cargo policy for the Manjung power station.
On arrival the mitre joints between unwound fifth limbs and the yoke had separated from prolonged vessel motion in winter gales.
Insurers denied the claim citing inherent vice; repair costs exceeded £1 million.
Force 8 winds and significant wave heights over 6 metres for extended periods occurred on ordinary January short-sea passages.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Insurers' claim for declaration of non-liability under project marine cargo policy.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration granted; loss caused by inability to withstand ordinary voyage incidents, not unusual perils of the sea.
enrichment.ratio: Under an all-risks cargo policy excluding inherent vice, the insured must prove loss by external fortuitous accident; where winter gale conditions on UK-Malaysia routes are ordinary incidents of the voyage and the cargo progressively fails from normal pitching and rolling, the proximate cause is inherent vice rather than perils of the sea.
legal_issues: Whether transformer damage was proximately caused by perils of the sea or inherent vice
Meaning of all-risks cover and insured's burden of proof
Whether prolonged force 8 conditions were extraordinary for the voyage
Application of Gaunt and Noten v Harding to packing and natural behaviour of goods
linked_authorities: British and Foreign Marine Insurance Co Ltd v Gaunt [1921] 2 AC 41
Soya GmbH Mainz KG v White [1983] 1 Lloyd's Rep 122
TM Noten BV v Harding [1990] 2 Lloyd's Rep 283

confidence.notes: Detailed findings on mechanism of failure and weather normality support clear inherent vice conclusion.
